item.title: Predicting transcriptional interactions with GrnPFN
item.description: arXiv:2611.14559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combinatorial therapies offer opportunities to improve treatment efficacy and overcome therapeutic resistance, but their rational design requires understanding how combined interventions interact beyond their individual effects. Combined genetic and chemical perturbations can elicit nonadditive transcriptional responses, yet the vast number of possible combinations limits experimental characterization. Predicting these interactions is particularly challenging when few or no combinations have been measured. Here we present GrnPFN, a prior-data fitted network that predicts nonadditive transcriptional responses to combinations from single-perturbation profiles. Pretrained on simulated screens generated from random gene-regulatory networks, GrnPFN incorporates measured combinations through in-context learning without retraining. We evaluated GrnPFN in single-cell screens spanning CRISPR activation, RNA knockdown and drug combinations, using separate cells to construct model inputs, training targets and test targets. Without measured combinations in the target screen, GrnPFN outperformed gradient boosting trained on other screens. With limited combination measurements, it outperformed kernel ridge regression fitted to the same measured pairs. These advantages extended to an additional screen combining CRISPR interference with a drug. Our results demonstrate that pretraining on simulated regulatory networks enables prediction of nonadditive transcriptional interactions across perturbation modalities when experimental measurements are scarce.
item.dc:creator: Haihui Zhang

item.title: PathwayDesigner: an interactive SBML/KEGG/Reactome/Escher compatible editor for biochemical network diagrams
item.description: arXiv:2611.14930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: PathwayDesigner is an interactive editor for biochemical network diagrams. A network can be drawn directly on the screen, or described as an Antimony model, which PathwayDesigner then lays out and draws. PathwayDesigner reads and writes SBML using the Layout and Render packages, writing Render in a form that other tools can interpret correctly. PathwayDesigner can read and write a diagram's layout and appearance using either Antimony's own layout statements or in a new, more concise format that we propose. PathwayDesigner can also open Escher maps, KEGG maps and Reactome's SBML-based maps. Other components of the model, such as events, rules, functions, and units, are kept and can be edited within the application. Species and reactions can be annotated with references to any database, and PathwayDesigner can find and add annotation references automatically by searching the BiGG, ChEBI, PubChem, and Rhea databases with a component's Id or Display Name, or contextually with a reaction's reactants and products. The network's stoichiometry matrix, conservation laws, and flux null space are computed and visualized on the diagram. The visual style of a diagram can be set with named styles or themes, saved and reused across models. One built-in theme follows the Escher style. The software is written in pure Rust as one code base for Windows, macOS, Linux, and the web browser, where it runs as WebAssembly. The web version is hosted on a GitHub page so that a user doesn't need to manually install code. All 1,062 curated BioModels models and the 1,823 semantic cases of the SBML Test Suite were read and written back without change. Diagrams were exchanged in both directions with COPASI and SBMLNetwork. PathwayDesigner is released as open source with MIT licence, at https://github.com/sys-bio/PathwayDesigner-rs, and runs in the browser at https://sys-bio.github.io/PathwayDesigner-rs/.
item.dc:creator: Herbert M. Sauro

item.title: The impact of DNA replication on the timing of cellular events
item.description: arXiv:2611.15356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cellular timing often relies on the accumulation of a regulatory protein to a threshold. For a stable protein produced at a constant rate, the threshold alone sets timing precision: the squared coefficient of variation of the first-passage time is the inverse of the threshold number of molecules. This counting limit appears to be a fundamental constraint. However, production rates vary across the cell cycle. By solving exactly a stochastic model coupling DNA replication and protein accumulation, we show that when a gene replicates at an optimal time, precision exceeds the counting limit.
item.dc:creator: Juan David Marmolejo-Lozano, Nikola Popovi\'c, Ramon Grima

item.title: A disease-contextualized atlas of proteome-scale molecular influences of natural products
item.description: arXiv:2611.15608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the system-wide molecular effects of natural products remains challenging because chemical knowledge is fragmented, proteomic coverage is incomplete, and experimental perturbation data are scarce, particularly for multicomponent medicinal herbs. Here we present an integrative framework for modeling molecular influences of natural compounds and medicinal herbs in disease-specific contexts. We harmonized three herbal medicine databases to establish a standardized atlas of 46,422 chemical entities, 12,459 medicinal herbs, and 156,588 herb-compound associations. We integrated high-confidence protein-protein interactions with proteomic and transcriptomic data to reconstruct molecular networks across nine cancers. By prioritizing protein-level evidence and using transcriptomic associations to extend coverage, these networks capture disease-associated interaction rewiring beyond differential expression. We coupled AI-inferred compound-target interactions with signed random walks with restart to model the propagation of molecular influences from sparse direct targets to directional, genome-scale network profiles. Using gastric cancer as an in-depth case study, we generated profiles for 45,418 compounds across 16,899 molecular nodes and explored multicomponent herbal interventions. We further applied the framework to eight additional cancers and retrospectively compared selected profiles with published drug-perturbation proteomics. This atlas provides a scalable basis for systems-level modeling of natural-product interventions and mechanism-guided drug discovery.
item.dc:creator: Boyang Wang, Jun Kang, Bo Zhang

item.title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
item.description: arXiv:2611.14540v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Cellitti, Lorenzo Di Rocco, Livia Perfetto, Veronica Lombardo, Umberto Ferraro Petrillo

item.title: Uncertainty-aware integration of deuterium metabolic imaging with genome-scale metabolic modeling reveals diet-associated feasible-space remodeling in mouse skeletal muscle
item.description: arXiv:2610.15175v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deuterium metabolic imaging (DMI) measures glucose-derived labeling in vivo, but noisy time courses complicate network-level interpretation. We developed an uncertainty-aware workflow that integrates dynamic DMI data with genome-scale metabolic modeling (GEM) through soft flux constraints. After injection of [6,6'-2H2]glucose, dynamic spectra were acquired from gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles of control and high-fat diet (HFD) mice. A hierarchical four-state kinetic model estimated labeling parameters while accounting for shared plasma input, tissue-specific kinetics, voxel-level fluxes, isotope effects, and measurement uncertainty. Because glucose labeling was more reliable than lactate and glutamate/glutamine signals, only two DMI-derived quantities were used as GEM anchors: glucose processing mapped to hexokinase flux, and glucose-derived oxidative entry mapped to mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase flux. Two-sided soft target intervals with weighted penalties defined DMI-compatible feasible regions for each mouse and muscle. Flux variability analysis and sampling assessed changes across reactions and metabolic subsystems. The constraints were compatible with the muscle network and affected feasible activity in glycolysis, lactate metabolism, pyruvate oxidation, the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and redox pathways. HFD-associated changes differed by muscle: tibialis anterior and soleus showed reduced glucose-linked feasible activity, whereas gastrocnemius showed mixed changes with preserved or increased TCA and redox activity. This framework connects noninvasive tracer imaging with network-level metabolic inference while avoiding strong claims from poorly identified signals.
item.dc:creator: Tin Yau Pang, Samia Maouhoub, Maruf Khan, Andreas Korzowski, Michael Roden, Ulrich Fl\"ogel, Daniel D\"orr

item.title: Spontaneous Spirals in Spatial Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.38710v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Several chemical and biological systems produce spontaneous spirals in their dynamical behavior, such as the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction in chemistry and the slime mold Dictyostelium in biology. In a previous study, such spiral wave formation was accurately replicated with a computational spatial system known as the Ideal Storage Cellular Automaton Model (ISCAM). Here, a more detailed investigation is presented of the ability of this model to generate spontaneous spirals depending on its parameter values. A dynamical systems analysis is performed, and bifurcation diagrams, phase space diagrams, and snapshots of the model's spatial dynamics are presented for a range of parameter values. This analysis reveals that spiral waves can only be sustained in the system when the parameter values of the model fall well within the regime of a so-called Neimark-Sacker bifurcation.
item.dc:creator: Wim Hordijk

item.title: Post-transcriptional Regulation of Stochastic Gene Expression Conditioned on Large Deviations
item.description: arXiv:2607.17004v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gene expression is a stochastic process that gives rise to large fluctuations in protein levels leading to phenotypic heterogeneity in clonal cell populations; post-transcriptional regulation plays a crucial role in controlling the level of phenotypic variability within a population, which is directly tied to cell-fate decisions. As such, substantial efforts have been directed towards quantitatively modeling the effects of various post-transcriptional mechanisms on the strength of fluctuations in protein levels (noise). However, the corresponding effects of post-transcriptional regulation on the occurrence of rare events corresponding to large deviations are far less explored and have only been considered for a special model. Here, we take a general model of post-transcriptional regulation and apply the partitioning of Poisson arrivals (PPA) framework to map it onto a model that resembles promoter-based regulation of transcription, leading to a general framework to obtain objects of interest in large deviations (i.e. large deviation rate function for quantifying the likelihood of observing rare protein production rates and the corresponding driven process that characterizes the system dynamics conditional on the rare event) for models of post-transcriptional regulation directly from prior results for promoter-based models. The results derived create new avenues to analyze rare events in general models of post-transcriptional regulation pertaining to various different biological settings.
item.dc:creator: Kenny Wong, Thomas Mourier, Cameron Hopkinson

item.title: PertReason: A Knowledge-Grounded Benchmark and Framework for Cell-State-Conditioned Mechanistic Reasoning of Perturbation Effects
item.description: arXiv:2607.18777v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Evaluating machine learning in scientific domains requires separating correct predictions from correct reasons under realistic distribution shifts. We introduce PertReason, a knowledge-grounded approach to evaluating and improving cell-state-conditioned reasoning about perturbation effects. Our framework comprises PertReasonQA, a benchmark that provides evaluation and supervision, and PertReasonLM, a reference large language model that demonstrates how such supervision supports reasoning-centric training. PertReasonQA tests whether models can generate mechanistically faithful explanations while remaining robust to complex shifts, such as new cells, unseen perturbations, cross-modal or combinatorial extrapolations. PertReasonQA combines single-cell genetic and chemical perturbation data across multiple cellular contexts with knowledge graphs, and dynamically conditions pathways on cell-specific basal states to avoid generic memorization. Evaluations of state-of-the-art models reveal systematic gaps between outcome prediction and mechanistic reasoning. As a reference probe of the benchmark, PertReasonLM is trained through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning using mechanistic supervision from PertReasonQA. PertReasonLM improves predictive accuracy and reduces answer-reason disagreement by grounding rationales in context-specific pathways. Together, we provide a diagnostic framework for exposing and mitigating failures in faithful reasoning in data-rich scientific systems. We release our datasets to support further research at https://dongkwan-kim.github.io/PertReason/.
item.dc:creator: Dongkwan Kim, Yiming Gao, Yining Yang, Yang Shen
